Choosing an outsourced ASNT Level III of record in Houston: certificates, examinations, sign-offs and conflicts

An ASNT Level III of record is the person your written practice names as its technical authority: the one who approves procedures, prepares and grades Level I and II examinations, and answers an auditor's technical questions. For Houston contractors and operators, the harder decision is whom to trust with that signature. This section sets out what to check before you sign an agreement with an NDT Level 3 consultant, and how the role works when Atlantis holds it.

What does the Level III of record sign?

  • The written practice and its revisions, including the designation of the Level III by name.
  • Each NDT procedure and technique sheet in the methods the Level III holds, with the code edition and acceptance criteria stated.
  • General, specific and practical examinations: question banks, practical specimens with known discontinuities, grading, and the certification recommendation the employer then signs.
  • Procedure demonstrations, when a code, an operator or a purchaser wants a technique proven on a representative sample.

For radiography, the Level III approves procedures and reviews the images produced by your licensed radiography contractor. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US.

SNT-TC-1A or CP-189: does the certificate matter?

Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own Level III, so a Level III of record can in principle be employer-certified. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 is stricter and requires the Level III to hold a current ASNT NDT Level III certificate. Some owners and contractors write CP-189 or ASNT certification into their contracts, so check what your customers name before choosing. ASNT Level III certificates are renewed every five years: ask for the certificate number and expiry date, and confirm them with ASNT.

Who offers a Level III of record in Houston?

  • Salaried in-house Level IIIs at large contractors and some operators. Continuity is strong; the risk is one person covering methods they are not certified in.
  • Texas NDT schools on retainer. NDTCS in Houston describes Level III retainers that give smaller companies periodic advice and audits, and TXNDT describes a renewing retainer plus representation with customers and auditors.
  • National inspection companies. Mistras offers appointment of its own Level IIIs as a client's representative for code and specification compliance, alongside its inspection work.
  • Independent and remote outsourced Level IIIs, who can review a contractor's results at arm's length because they are not supplying that contractor's labour.

Vetting questions to put to any ASNT Level III consultant

  1. Show me the ASNT certificate. Which methods does it list, and when does it expire?
  2. Who covers the signature while you are on another client's audit or travelling? Name the backup and their methods.
  3. Do you supply inspectors to us, or to our competitors on the same unit? If so, how is your independence protected?
  4. Where are answer sheets, examination records and practical specimen data kept, and who owns them if the agreement ends?
  5. How will you administer and record vision examinations for technicians spread across several sites?
  6. Will you demonstrate the procedure on our specimen rather than a generic block?

What happens when you change your Level III of record?

A change is a revision event, not a phone call. The written practice is revised to name the new Level III; open procedures are reviewed and re-approved under the new signature; the examination banks and practical specimen records transfer to the employer, who owns them; and certifications issued under the old Level III generally remain valid, provided they were issued correctly under the written practice in force at the time; the employer's written practice decides. Plan the hand-over before an audit, so the auditor sees one continuous record.
